PTFE Seals · Sealing

PTFE Seals & O-Rings

Machined PTFE (Teflon) O-rings, back-up rings, lip seals and V-packing for media, temperatures and speeds that defeat rubber seals — made to standard groove sizes or your drawing.

Request a Quote WhatsApp

PTFE seals step in where elastomers fail: aggressive chemicals, very low or very high temperatures, dry running and long periods without maintenance. The trade-off is that PTFE is not rubbery, so a good PTFE seal is designed around how the material actually behaves. SK Polymers machines PTFE seals to size from virgin and filled stock.

Types of PTFE seal

General guidance — the right seal depends on pressure, speed, temperature, media and the hardware.
SealHow it worksTypical use
PTFE O-ringA solid PTFE ring squeezed in a groove; seals by compression rather than elastic recoveryStatic seals in chemical service, where rubber would swell or degrade
PTFE back-up ringA stiff ring fitted beside an elastomer O-ring to close the clearance gapHydraulic and high-pressure seals, to stop the O-ring extruding
PTFE lip sealA PTFE lip held against a shaft, sometimes with a spring or support ringRotary shafts running dry, fast or in aggressive media
PTFE V-packingA stack of chevron rings; tightening the gland spreads the lips onto shaft and borePump plungers, valve stems and reciprocating rods

PTFE O-rings

A solid PTFE O-ring does not stretch and spring back like rubber, so it cannot be rolled into a closed groove and does not recover if the joint opens up. That makes it best suited to static seals with a good surface finish and steady clamping. Where you need PTFE’s chemical resistance and elasticity, spring-energised PTFE seals or fluoropolymer-encapsulated O-rings are the usual alternatives.

PTFE back-up rings

Under high pressure an elastomer O-ring can be forced into the gap between the mating parts and torn — known as extrusion. A PTFE back-up ring on the low-pressure side bridges that gap. They are supplied solid, split (scarf-cut) or spiral; split and spiral rings are easier to fit into closed grooves.

PTFE V-packing

V-packing sets combine several PTFE chevron rings with male and female adapters. Because the gland can be tightened as the rings wear, V-packing is forgiving in reciprocating and slow-rotating service such as pump plungers and valve stems.

Grades for seals

Virgin PTFE is preferred for the widest chemical resistance and for low-pressure static seals. Filled grades resist extrusion and wear better: glass-filled is a common general-purpose seal grade, carbon-filled suits water and steam, bronze-filled is widely used for hydraulic back-up and guide rings, and graphite-filled lowers friction against softer shafts. See virgin vs filled PTFE and the chemical resistance guide.

Applications

  • Rotary and reciprocating shafts — lip seals and V-packing on mixers, agitators and plungers.
  • Chemical pumps — seals and wear rings where media attack elastomers; see also PTFE bushes.
  • Cryogenic service — PTFE remains usable at temperatures where most rubbers turn brittle.
  • High-temperature valves — stem packings and seat seals in hot, aggressive service.
  • Hydraulic back-up rings — protecting O-rings in high-pressure cylinders and valves.
  • Flange and body seals — where a ring or PTFE gasket suits the joint better than an O-ring.

Design notes for PTFE seals

Typical values for unfilled (virgin) PTFE, compiled from published material data. Actual values depend on resin, processing and test method — they are a design guide, not a specification for a particular lot.
Continuous service temperatureapprox. −200 °C to +260 °C
Elongation at breakapprox. 250 – 400 %
Hardnessapprox. 50 – 60 Shore D
Coefficient of friction (dynamic, on steel)approx. 0.05 – 0.10
Thermal expansionhigh — roughly ten times that of steel at room temperature

Three behaviours shape every PTFE seal design. PTFE creeps, so sealing force relaxes unless something — a spring, an elastomer or an adjustable gland — keeps it loaded. Its thermal expansion is high, so fits change with temperature. And its low friction means low breakaway and running torque, one reason PTFE suits seals that run dry. Hardware surface finish matters too: a smooth, hard counterface extends seal life. Read more in the PTFE properties guide.

What to include in your enquiry

  1. Seal type, or the hardware and duty so we can suggest one.
  2. Groove or housing dimensions, shaft or bore size — or the drawing.
  3. Pressure, temperature range and media.
  4. Static, rotary or reciprocating motion, with speed if dynamic.
  5. Grade preference and quantity.

Common Questions

PTFE Seal FAQs

Questions buyers commonly ask before ordering PTFE seals and O-rings.

Ask a Question

Sometimes. A solid PTFE O-ring resists chemicals and temperature far better, but it is not elastic, so it suits static seals with steady clamping. For dynamic duty or where elasticity is needed, consider a spring-energised PTFE seal.

It sits beside an elastomer O-ring on the low-pressure side and bridges the clearance gap, preventing the O-ring from being extruded and damaged under high pressure.

Solid rings give the most support but need an open groove to fit. Split (scarf-cut) and spiral rings can be fitted into closed grooves more easily. Tell us the groove type and pressure and we will suggest one.

PTFE remains usable at very low temperatures where most rubbers become brittle, which is why it is common in cryogenic valve seals. Seal design still has to allow for the large dimensional change on cooling.

Teflon™ is a Chemours brand name for PTFE, and “Teflon seal” is commonly used to mean a PTFE seal. We supply PTFE seals; we do not claim they are the branded product.
